<a id="pm-s1"></a>
## 1. Abstract and result contract

> We give a negative solution to the finite lattice representation problem. We prove that there is a finite nonempty lattice that is not the full congruence lattice of any finite nonempty algebra of any finite signature.

- **claim-finite-congruence-obstruction** (theorem, [source](#stmt-main-congruences)): There exists a finite nonempty lattice $L$ such that $$L\not\cong\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}(A)$$ for every finite nonempty algebra $A$ of every finite signature.
  - Explanation: Some finite nonempty lattice has no representation as the entire congruence lattice of any finite nonempty algebra, even when the finite signature may vary.
- **claim-finite-group-interval-obstruction** (theorem, [source](#stmt-main-group)): There exists a finite lattice that is not isomorphic to $[D,G]$ for any subgroup $D$ of any finite group $G$.
  - Explanation: Some finite lattice cannot occur as an entire subgroup interval of any finite group.
- **claim-fenced-normal-subgroup-test** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-frm-normal-test)): Suppose that $[D,X]$ is fenced. If $R\trianglelefteq X$, then either $R\le D$ or $DR=X$. In particular, $[D,X]$ is not modular. The same assertion applies to a normal subgroup of $X/F$ whenever $F\trianglelefteq X$ and $F\le D$, with bottom $D/F$.
  - Explanation: A fence forces every normal subgroup either into the bottom or to supplement it, and the same test survives the specified quotient.
- **claim-unique-nonabelian-socle-label** (classification, [source](#stmt-frm-labels)): Suppose that $[D,X]$ is fenced, and put $$F_X=\operatorname{core}_X(D) =\bigcap_{g\in X}D^g.$$ Then $X/F_X$ has a unique minimal normal subgroup $$\label{frm:socle-label} S_X=N_X/F_X\cong T_X^{m_X},$$ where $T_X$ is nonabelian simple and $N_X$ is its full inverse image in $X$. Moreover, $$X=DN_X.$$ Every nontrivial normal subgroup of $X/F_X$ contains $S_X$, and $$C_{X/F_X}(S_X)=1.$$ In particular, $X/F_X$ has no nontrivial soluble normal subgroup. If $I_X$ is the set of simple direct factors of $S_X$, then $D$ and $X$ induce the same transitive permutation group on $I_X$.
  - Explanation: A fenced vertex has a unique nonabelian minimal normal subgroup modulo its bottom core, with faithful conjugation and matching transitive factor actions from the bottom and the vertex.
- **claim-labelled-bottleneck-normal-tests** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-frm-bottleneck)): Let $D<B\le Z$, suppose that $[D,B]$ is fenced, and suppose that $B$ is comparable with every member of $[D,Z]$. If $R\trianglelefteq Z$ and $R\nleq D$, then $$B=D(R\cap B).$$ Consequently a soluble normal subgroup of $Z$ is contained in $D$. If $R,Q\trianglelefteq Z$ and $$[R,Q]\le F\trianglelefteq Z,\qquad F\le D,$$ then at least one of $R,Q$ is contained in $D$. These conclusions also hold with $B=Z$.
  - Explanation: A labelled bottleneck controls soluble normal subgroups and commuting normal subgroups in the larger interval without asserting a full supplementation dichotomy there.
- **claim-subdirect-diagonal-strip-classification** (classification, [source](#stmt-frm-subdirect)): Let $T$ be nonabelian simple. Every subdirect subgroup $E\le T^I$ is a direct product of full diagonal strips on the parts of a partition of $I$. Both the partition and the coordinate identifications within each part are determined by $E$. An inclusion of subdirect subgroups corresponds to a refinement of these parts, with the existing identifications restricted to the smaller parts.
  - Explanation: Subdirect powers of a nonabelian simple group are determined by diagonal strips and their coordinate identifications; containment refines the strip partition.
- **claim-equal-type-coordinate-transport** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-frm-equal-transport)): Let $D<X<Y$ be labelled vertices. Then $F_Y\le F_X$, and $T_X$ is isomorphic to a section of $T_Y$. Put $$E_X=(X\cap N_Y)/F_Y\le S_Y.$$ The following conditions are equivalent:* 1. *$T_X\cong T_Y$;* 2. *$E_X$ is subdirect in $S_Y$.* *When they hold, the quotient map induces an isomorphism $$\label{frm:equal-socle-identification} E_X\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }S_X, \qquad N_X=F_X(X\cap N_Y), \qquad F_X\cap N_Y=F_Y.$$ Moreover $m_X<m_Y$, and the strip supports give a canonical $X$-equivariant surjection $$\label{frm:equal-support-map} \sigma_{YX}:I_Y\longrightarrow I_X.$$ For three comparable labelled vertices of the same simple type these maps compose: $\sigma_{ZX}=\sigma_{YX}\sigma_{ZY}$.
  - Explanation: Equal simple types are equivalent to a subdirect socle trace. The resulting support maps decrease multiplicity strictly and compose along comparable vertices.
- **claim-strict-type-saturation** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-frm-strict-product)): Let $D\le X<Y$, where $Y$ is labelled. Suppose that the coordinate projections of $$B=(X\cap N_Y)/F_Y$$ are proper and nontrivial. If $[X,Y]$ is fenced, or if $X$ is a coatom of $[D,Y]$, then $X$ is saturated relative to $Y$.* *Once $B=P^{I_Y}$ is such a product, no proper subdirect subgroup of $S_Y$ contains $B$. Every coatom of $[X,Y]$, and every intersection of these coatoms, is saturated relative to $Y$. These assertions do not require $X$ to be labelled. For labelled $X<Y$ of different simple types the projection hypothesis holds.
  - Explanation: Proper nontrivial coordinate projections become a full coordinate product under the fence or coatom hypothesis. Coatoms above that product and their intersections remain saturated.
- **claim-entire-one-coordinate-interval** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-frm-projection)): Let $D\le X<Y$, with $Y$ labelled, and suppose that $$(X\cap N_Y)/F_Y=P_X^{I_Y},\qquad 1<P_X<T_Y.$$ Suppose also that $X$ is an intersection of coatoms of $[X,Y]$; a coatom itself is allowed. Fix $i\in I_Y$ and let $$\rho:Y_i\longrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}(T_Y)$$ be the action of its factor stabilizer on that coordinate. Identify $T_Y$ with its inner automorphism group, and put $H_* = \rho(X_i)$. Then $$\label{frm:inner-bottom} H_*\cap T_Y=P_X.$$ The saturated overgroups of $X$ form a sublattice of $[X,Y]$, and $$\label{frm:coordinate-interval} Z\longmapsto K_Z=\rho(Z_i)=H_*P_Z, \qquad (Z\cap N_Y)/F_Y=P_Z^{I_Y},$$ is an isomorphism from that sublattice onto the entire ordinary subgroup interval $[H_*,H_*T_Y]$. Original covering relations between saturated vertices remain covering relations after projection. In particular, a strict change of simple type at a cover yields a maximal subgroup of an almost simple group, supplementing its simple socle.
  - Explanation: Saturation and the coatom-intersection hypothesis give an entire ordinary subgroup interval after projection, with the actual factor-stabilizer image as bottom and with original covers preserved.
- **claim-active-chief-factor-transport** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-frm-active-transport)): Let $D<Z\le Y$ be labelled vertices, and suppose that $Z$ is saturated relative to $Y$: $$(Z\cap N_Y)/F_Y=P_Z^{I_Y}.$$ Let $K_Z$ be the automorphism group induced by a factor stabilizer in $Z$ on a reference coordinate of $S_Y$. There are $K_Z$-normal subgroups $Q_Z\le R_Z\le P_Z$ such that $$\begin{aligned} \label{frm:product-core} (F_Z\cap N_Y)/F_Y&=Q_Z^{I_Y},\\ \label{frm:product-active-preimage} (N_Z\cap N_Y)/F_Y&=R_Z^{I_Y},\\ \label{frm:coordinate-chief} R_Z/Q_Z&\cong T_Z^{a_Z},\qquad m_Z=a_Zm_Y. \end{aligned}$$ Here $a_Z$ is a positive integer. The section $R_Z/Q_Z$ is a chief factor for the action of $K_Z$ on $P_Z$: there is no $K_Z$-normal subgroup strictly between $Q_Z$ and $R_Z$. Its factors give a $Z$-equivariant surjection $$\label{frm:product-support} \tau_{ZY}:I_Z\longrightarrow I_Y$$ whose fibers have size $a_Z$. The stabilizers in $D$ and $Z$ of a coordinate in $I_Y$ induce the same transitive action on its fiber.* *In addition, suppose $X<Z$ and the hypotheses of Proposition <a href="#frm:projection" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="frm:projection">10</a> hold for $X<Y$. Set $$H_* = \rho(X_i),\qquad K_Z=H_*P_Z, \qquad C_Z=\operatorname{core}_{K_Z}(H_*).$$ Then the subgroups in <a href="#frm:product-core" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="frm:product-core">[frm:product-core]</a> satisfy $$\label{frm:projected-core} Q_Z=C_Z\cap P_Z, \qquad K_Z=H_*R_Z.$$ Thus $R_ZC_Z/C_Z\cong R_Z/Q_Z$ is a transitive minimal normal subgroup in the coset action of $K_Z/C_Z$ on $H_*/C_Z$. The groups $H_*$ and $K_Z$ induce the same action on its simple factors. No assertion that this is the entire projected socle is required.* *If $a_Z=1$, the quotient $P_Z/R_Z$ is soluble.
  - Explanation: Original cores and active socle preimages split into coordinate products. The active chief factor supplies a support map and full local factor actions; the additional projected-core identity requires a strictly higher vertex.
- **claim-absolute-tested-chain-rigidity** (bound, [source](#stmt-cls-chain-rigidity)): There is an absolute integer $B$ such that every tested chain of length $N\geq B$ satisfies $T_a\cong T_b$.
  - Explanation: The endpoint simple types of a sufficiently long tested chain agree, with a threshold independent of all ambient finite-group parameters.
- **claim-maximal-subgroup-literature-inputs** (classification, [source](#stmt-cls-literature)): The following results are used from the classification and representation theory of finite simple groups.* 1. *A maximal subgroup of an almost simple classical group, not containing its socle, is a stabilizer in one of Aschbacher’s eight geometric collections, or has an almost simple irreducible component. The geometric collections are subspace or flag stabilizers, direct-sum decompositions, extension-field structures, tensor products, subfield structures, symplectic-type groups, tensor-induced decompositions, and forms. Graph automorphisms may interchange the relevant subspaces or flag members; triality and exceptional graph–field automorphisms occur only in bounded rank. We use (Aschbacher 1984) [[Aschbacher1984](#ref-Aschbacher1984)] and the almost simple formulation and descriptions in (Kleidman and Liebeck 1990, Table 1.2.A and Theorem 1.2.1, pp. 3–4) [[KleidmanLiebeck1990](#ref-KleidmanLiebeck1990)], with the geometric descriptions in Chapters 3–5; the connected tensor structures and their finite fixed-point versions are also given in (Liebeck and Seitz 1998, Theorem 2 and Section 4(5)) [[LiebeckSeitzClassical1998](#ref-LiebeckSeitzClassical1998)].* 2. *The maximal subgroups of alternating and symmetric groups have the intransitive, imprimitive, affine, diagonal, product-action, or almost simple alternatives of the maximal-subgroup form of the O’Nan–Scott Theorem. The relevant formulation and all the alternatives used here are recorded in the proof of (Burness, Liebeck, and Shalev 2017, Proposition 3.1) [[BurnessLiebeckShalev2017](#ref-BurnessLiebeckShalev2017)].* 3. *For a fixed algebraic type, sufficiently general finite subgroups lie between the derived group and the inner-diagonal group of a finite fixed-point group. The complementary alternative is containment in a proper algebraic subgroup of bounded complexity. The bounded-envelope version permits passage to the reductive simple quotients of that subgroup; see (Larsen and Pink 2011, Theorems 0.5 and 12.3) [[LarsenPink2011](#ref-LarsenPink2011)].* 4. *A subgroup maximal in a maximal subgroup of an almost simple group has at most five nonabelian chief factors (Burness, Liebeck, and Shalev 2017, Proposition 8.1) [[BurnessLiebeckShalev2017](#ref-BurnessLiebeckShalev2017)]. The number refers to chief factors, not to their simple direct factors.* 5. *If $[H,A]$ is a height-two interval and $A$ is alternating or symmetric of degree at least five, it has at most eleven interior vertices (Basile 2001, Theorem D) [[Basile2008](#ref-Basile2008)]. Here the entire interval is required to have height two: $H$ is maximal in every maximal overgroup. This is the hypothesis imposed whenever the result is used.* 6. *Cross-characteristic irreducible projective degrees satisfy the Landazuri–Seitz lower bounds (Landazuri and Seitz 1974) [[LandazuriSeitz1974](#ref-LandazuriSeitz1974)]. In particular, outside bounded rank, a source of natural dimension $n$ and field parameter $q$ requires degree at least $q^{c n}$ for an absolute $c>0$; the applicable classical bounds are recorded in (Häsä 2014, Tables 3–6) [[Hasa2014](#ref-Hasa2014)]. Above an absolute classical rank, every perfect central cover of a finite simple classical group is a central quotient of its usual simply connected fixed-point group, uniformly over all finite fields, including the standard graph twists (Steinberg 1981, Theorem 1.1 and p. 528) [[Steinberg1981](#ref-Steinberg1981)]. The central-cover deduction and preservation of representations are proved in Lemma <a href="#lift:finite-covers" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lift:finite-covers">44</a>. After passing to that cover, defining-characteristic irreducibles have the Steinberg highest-weight and tensor-product parametrization (Steinberg 1963, Theorems 1.1 and 1.3) [[Steinberg1963](#ref-Steinberg1963)], including the twisted fixed-point groups (Steinberg 1967, Theorem 43) [[SteinbergNotes](#ref-SteinbergNotes)].
  - Explanation: The proof uses the stated maximal-subgroup alternatives, bounded envelopes, chief-factor and interval bounds, degree estimates, and central-cover representation results under their separate hypotheses.
- **claim-bounded-depth-active-factor-actions** (bound, [source](#stmt-cls-cat-actions)): Consider a strict labelled cover and its one-coordinate maximal subgroup $M$ in an almost simple group, as supplied by Proposition <a href="#frm:projection" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="frm:projection">10</a>. Mark its active nonabelian chief factor. There are absolute positive integers $b_0,r_0$ with the following property.* 1. *The action on the simple factors of the marked chief factor is obtained through at most $r_0$ transitive action levels. Each level either has degree at most $b_0$, or is the natural action of $A_d$ or $S_d$.
  - Explanation: An active chief-factor action at a strict labelled cover has bounded depth, with bounded-degree levels or full natural alternating and symmetric levels.
- **claim-bounded-stabilizer-routes** (bound, [source](#stmt-cls-routes)): Fix positive integers $r,b$. Suppose $$A=H_r\leq H_{r-1}\leq\cdots\leq H_0=H$$ and every induced action on $H_{j-1}/H_j$ is either of degree at most $b$ or is a natural alternating or symmetric action. There are constants $h,c,k$, depending only on $r,b$, such that:* 1. *the interval $[A,H]$ has height at most $h$;* 2. *the set $\{[H:U]:A\leq U\leq H\}$ has cardinality at most $k$;* 3. *for every such $U$, its nonabelian composition types belong to $$\operatorname{cf}_{\mathrm{na}}(H) \cup\{A_{d-j}:A_d\in\operatorname{cf}_{\mathrm{na}}(H),\ 0\leq j\leq c\} \cup\mathcal E_{r,b},$$ where $\mathcal E_{r,b}$ is a fixed finite set of types.* *The conclusions also hold for stabilizers of all invariant quotient blocks of the action on $H/A$.
  - Explanation: A bounded route of small or natural giant actions controls interval height, possible indices, and nonabelian composition types, including invariant quotient-block stabilizers.
- **claim-common-index-recipe-palette** (bound, [source](#stmt-cls-index-recipes)): Fix positive integers $R,b,K$. Consider any collection of the routes in Lemma <a href="#cls:routes" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cls:routes">17</a>, each of length at most $R$ and bounded degree at most $b$, such that all their natural giant degrees belong to one set $\mathcal D$ with $\|\mathcal D\|\leq K$. The union, over all groups and routes in the collection, of all indices $[H:U]$ with $A\leq U\leq H$ has cardinality bounded by a function of $R,b,K$. The same holds through a bounded number of operations, each consisting of a permitted route followed by an arbitrary invariant quotient-block choice, with a fresh route inside the chosen block stabilizer permitted at the next operation.
  - Explanation: A common bounded set of giant degrees yields a bounded union of index values across all permitted routes and bounded sequences of route and block operations.
- **claim-uniform-projected-active-actions** (bound, [source](#stmt-cls-uniform-actions)): Suppose a tested chain has $T_a\not\cong T_b$, and project at one coordinate of the socle of $b$. Let $H_*$ be the image of the factor stabilizer in $a$. Then:* 1. *$H_*$ has at most five nonabelian chief factors;* 2. *there is one set of nonabelian types, of absolutely bounded cardinality, which contains the types of every whole projected stabilizer group in $H_*$ of an active factor, of an intermediate fiber, or of an invariant quotient block used along a two-edge shortcut, and the types of all their induced images;* 3. *equal-type stretches of chain vertices have absolutely bounded length;* 4. *the set of ratios $m_{x_i}/m_{x_j}$, $i<j$, has absolutely bounded cardinality after equal-type repetitions are removed.
  - Explanation: The fixed projected bottom controls all relevant projected stabilizer types, equal-type stretches, and the union of multiplicity ratios; it does not control entire unprojected stabilizers.
- **claim-soluble-killed-core-gaps** (bound, [source](#stmt-cls-core-gaps)): In the initial projection, consider chain vertices strictly above the original starting vertex $a$, and write $$K_i=H_*P_i,\qquad C_i=\operatorname{core}_{K_i}(H_*), \qquad Q_i=C_i\cap P_i,$$ and let $R_i/Q_i$ be its active nonabelian chief factor. For $i<j$, the inner comparison and its killed kernel are $$J_{ij}=(P_i\cap R_j)/Q_j, \qquad B_{ij}=(Q_i\cap R_j)/Q_j.$$ There is an embedding $B_{ij}\hookrightarrow C_i/C_j$. After deleting at most five nonsoluble gaps, an arbitrarily long subchain remains on which all the $B_{ij}$, including the analogous shortcut kernels, are soluble. If the chain multiplicities are equal, every endpoint inner comparison, projected to one factor of its upper active socle, has just its active simple factor as a nonabelian composition factor.
  - Explanation: Killed comparison kernels embed in descending projected-core quotients. Removing the bounded nonsoluble gaps leaves soluble kernels, and equal multiplicities leave only the active nonabelian factor in endpoint inner comparisons.
- **claim-large-alternating-type-exclusion** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-cls-alternating)): For $u\in\mathcal U$ with $T_a\not\cong T_u$, the type $T_u$ is not alternating of degree at least seven.
  - Explanation: The entire tested height-two interval excludes large alternating upper types when the original starting type differs.
- **claim-fixed-type-bounded-envelopes** (classification, [source](#stmt-cls-envelopes)): Fix a connected adjoint simple algebraic type $\Phi$. There is a constant $c_\Phi$ such that a finite subgroup $P$ of an algebraic group $X$ of type $\Phi$ has one of the following descriptions.* 1. *For a Frobenius map $F_0$, $$E=(X^{F_0})'\leq P\leq X^{F_0},$$ where $E$ is simple.* 2. *Every nonabelian composition factor of $P$ of order greater than $c_\Phi$ is of Lie type in the characteristic of $X$, with algebraic dimension strictly less than $\dim X$. The total number of nonabelian composition factors, counted with multiplicity, is at most $c_\Phi$.* *In particular, the ranks of nonabelian simple sections of finite groups of Lie type of rank at most $R$ are bounded by a function of $R$; simple sections of bounded order are included in this bound.
  - Explanation: A finite subgroup in a fixed adjoint algebraic type is either sufficiently general in a fixed-point group or has controlled smaller-dimensional nonabelian factors. This bounds ranks of simple sections in bounded ambient rank.
- **claim-normalized-prime-subfield-steps** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-cls-subfields)): Fix an adjoint simple type $\Phi$. Let $T=(X^F)'$ be simple, $T\leq A\leq\operatorname{Aut}(T)$, and let $M<A$ be maximal with $T\not\leq M$. Suppose that $P=M\cap T$ is in alternative (i) of Lemma <a href="#cls:envelopes" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cls:envelopes">22</a>, and that the parameter of $F_0$ is large enough in terms of $\Phi$. Then $F=F_0^r$ for a prime $r$. Every element of $M$ normalizes the derived fixed-point groups for all intermediate powers of $F_0$.
  - Explanation: A sufficiently large fixed-type subfield subgroup at a maximal step comes from a prime Frobenius power, and its normalizer preserves the intermediate fixed-point groups.
- **claim-bounded-rank-type-count** (bound, [source](#stmt-cls-bounded-rank)): For every $R$ there is $b(R)$ such that at most $b(R)$ distinct Lie types of rank at most $R$ occur in a tested chain after the alternating exclusion. In an arbitrarily long family of such chains with distinct types, one may therefore require the ranks of all retained endpoints and all their shortcut middles to exceed any prescribed constant.
  - Explanation: Only boundedly many distinct bounded-rank Lie types occur after the alternating exclusion, so arbitrarily long distinct-type chains can retain only endpoints and shortcut middles above any fixed rank threshold.
- **claim-classical-one-factor-reduction** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-cls-reduction)): If Theorem <a href="#cls:chain-rigidity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cls:chain-rigidity">14</a> is false, then for every $s$ and $R$ there is a retained chain of at least $s$ vertices, with all its original two-edge shortcuts and normal-group tests, such that:* 1. *all endpoint types are distinct classical types; their ranks, and the ranks of all shortcut middle types, exceed $R$;* 2. *all endpoint multiplicities are equal. Thus each comparison, projected to one upper active coordinate, has one active simple factor;* 3. *the killed kernels of all endpoint and shortcut comparisons are soluble. Every endpoint inner comparison has exactly its one active simple factor as a nonabelian composition factor;* 4. *there is a pool of absolutely bounded cardinality containing all nonabelian simple types in every projected active-factor and fiber stabilizer in the fixed $H_*$, and in their induced images, used in these comparisons. No assertion concerns the entire unprojected original stabilizers. The splitting multiplicities and invariant-block indices have boundedly many possible values;* 5. *each shortcut is either two strict steps, both with one active simple factor and all other inner composition factors soluble, or a strict split followed downwards by an equal-type merge. The latter is geometric. In geometric steps the inactive dimensions have boundedly many possible values once their simple labels and bounded structural choices are fixed; when all inactive components are soluble these dimensions are absolutely bounded.* *All bounds described as absolute are uniform over the original groups. This proposition introduces no new lattice tests at the retained bottom.
  - Explanation: Failure of chain rigidity yields retained large-rank classical chains with distinct endpoint types, equal multiplicities, soluble killed kernels, and bounded pools for projected stabilizers and geometric splitting data.
- **claim-classical-maximal-step-estimates** (classification, [source](#stmt-cls-cat-cross)): Consider a strict labelled cover and its one-coordinate maximal subgroup $M$ in an almost simple group with socle $T$, as supplied by Proposition <a href="#frm:projection" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="frm:projection">10</a>. Mark its active nonabelian chief factor. The non-geometric irreducible category below means that its simple source acts absolutely irreducibly on the ambient natural module and that the maximal subgroup is outside all geometric collections, in particular the subfield collection. All growing-rank assertions refer to growing *source* rank. There are absolute constants $C,c>0$ with the following properties.* 1. * For unbounded-rank classical active types, a geometric defining-characteristic step changes natural dimension by taking a subspace or quotient, a repeated natural module, a tensor product, or restriction of scalars. Subfield steps leave natural dimension unchanged and multiply the field exponent by a prime. An extension-field step, read upwards from the active factor, has $$\label{grw:matrix-field-convention} n_t=b n_s,\qquad \epsilon_s f_s=b\epsilon_t f_t, \qquad f_t=\frac{\epsilon_s}{b\epsilon_t}f_s,$$ where $b$ is the prime degree between natural matrix fields. A twisted-tensor step has $$\label{grw:twisted-field-convention} n_t=n_s^b,\qquad f_s=b f_t,$$ exactly; here $b$ is prime, after bounded source-rank cases are removed. All other changes of field exponent belong to a fixed finite set of positive rational factors.* 2. * If there is one active simple component and the other geometric components are soluble, their natural dimensions are absolutely bounded. The active dimension in a subspace case is comparable with the ambient dimension; a totally singular summand and its dual may represent the same active component twice. A nontrivial parabolic radical in these cases has order between $q^{c n_t}$ and $q^{C n_t^2}$. For a fixed ambient group, once the active slot, other component dimensions, and the bounded flag/form choices are fixed, there are boundedly many possible orders of the full inner stabilizer divided by the order of its active simple factor, with multiplicity included.* 3. * A symplectic-type step of unbounded active rank is cross-characteristic. Its source is symplectic or orthogonal over a prime field of order $r$, of natural dimension $2d+O(1)$, and its target natural dimension is $n_t=r^d$. If $P=M\cap T$, then $$c n_t^2\leq \|P\|/\|T_s\|\leq C n_t^2.$$ Its target field exponent is at most $\|T_s\|^C$.* 4. * After the twisted-tensor case in <a href="#cls:cat-geometric" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cls:cat-geometric">[cls:cat-geometric]</a> is separated off, a defining-characteristic almost simple irreducible step has a single nonzero restricted, nonnatural Frobenius digit, up to a common Frobenius twist. This restricted module may have further tensor factors in a very special characteristic. Its dimension is at least $c n_s^2$. Its source and target field exponents differ by a rational factor from a fixed finite set. Natural, dual-natural, and natural-size special-isogeny representations are included among the geometric cases instead.* 5. *For a cross-characteristic almost simple step, $$q_s^{c n_s}\leq n_t\leq \|T_s\|^C, \qquad f_t\leq \|T_s\|^C.$$ The upper degree bound also holds in defining characteristic. For this and the preceding irreducible case, the homomorphism from the ambient automorphism normalizer of the source simple group to its automorphism group has kernel of absolute bounded order. In particular, a subgroup of that normalizer has order at most $C$ times the order of its induced automorphism group of the source.
  - Explanation: The maximal-step classification distinguishes geometric, symplectic-type, defining-characteristic nonlinear, and cross-characteristic steps with their respective field, dimension, order, and normalizer constraints.
- **claim-irreducible-normalizer-kernel-bound** (bound, [source](#stmt-cls-normalizer)): In a non-geometric absolutely irreducible step of Proposition <a href="#cls:catalogue" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cls:catalogue">[cls:catalogue]</a>, let $Y$ denote the simple source inside the ambient projective classical group $T$. In particular, the maximal subgroup is not in a subfield collection. Then $$\bigl\|\ker\bigl(N_{\operatorname{Aut}(T)}(Y) \longrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}(Y)\bigr)\bigr\|\leq C$$ for an absolute $C$. Moreover $\|\operatorname{Out}(Y)\|\leq C n_Y f_Y$ for a large-rank classical source with parameters $(n_Y,p^{f_Y})$.
  - Explanation: Outside the subfield collection, the ambient automorphism normalizer of an absolutely irreducible source has uniformly bounded conjugation kernel. Large-rank classical outer automorphisms satisfy the stated parameter bound.
- **claim-prime-twisted-tensor-orbit** (classification, [source](#stmt-cls-twisted-tensor)): An almost simple irreducible maximal subgroup with a nontrivial Steinberg tensor decomposition is, in growing source rank, a geometric twisted-tensor step with the exact dimension and field relations in <a href="#cls:cat-geometric" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cls:cat-geometric">[cls:cat-geometric]</a>. Its tensor-orbit degree is prime.
  - Explanation: A nontrivial Steinberg tensor decomposition in a growing-rank maximal irreducible subgroup is geometric, with the exact usual-field and dimension relations and a prime tensor-cycle degree.
- **claim-coordinate-stabilizer-order-transport** (bound, [source](#stmt-grw-input-normalizers)): Suppose that the last cover is an almost simple irreducible cover with source $Y$, and that all three shortcut multiplicities agree, as in every application below. Denote the lower node’s full upper-coordinate stabilizer image by $M_{ij}$, and let $P_B$ be the inner projection in the first cover. Then $$\label{grw:normalizer-input} \|M_{ij}\|\le C\,\|P_B\|\,n'^{C}(1+f')^{C}.$$
  - Explanation: When the final cover is irreducible almost simple and shortcut multiplicities agree, the actual lower coordinate stabilizer is bounded using the first-cover inner projection and intermediate parameters.
- **claim-finite-prime-complexity-coloring** (bound, [source](#stmt-grw-prime-colors)): Let $x_1,\ldots,x_s$ be positive real numbers whose pair ratios are positive rationals. Suppose that, for every $i<j$, $$x_j/x_i=c_{ij}u_{ij}^{\varepsilon},\qquad c_{ij}\in\mathcal C,\qquad \varepsilon\in\{1,-1\},$$ where $\mathcal C$ is a fixed finite set of positive rationals, $u_{ij}$ is a positive integer with at most $h$ prime factors counted with multiplicity, and $\varepsilon$ is the same for all pairs. There is a number of colors depending only on $\mathcal C,h$ such that on every homogeneous triangle all three $x$’s are equal. Consequently arbitrarily long such arrays have arbitrarily long constant subarrays.
  - Explanation: A fixed rational correction palette and uniformly bounded prime complexity with a common valuation sign yield a finite coloring whose homogeneous triangles have constant values.
- **claim-opposite-field-move-exclusion** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-grw-opposite-fields)): Arbitrarily long homogeneous shortcut chains cannot have, on every comparison, one proper subfield step and one proper extension step, including the twisted-tensor extension alternative.
  - Explanation: Exact dimension relations exclude arbitrarily long homogeneous chains whose shortcuts combine proper subfield and proper extension moves, including twisted tensors.
- **claim-purely-geometric-path-exclusion** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-grw-no-geometric)): An arbitrarily long reduced chain cannot have exclusively geometric two-edge shortcuts. This includes strict split/equal-type merge shortcuts.
  - Explanation: A fixed lower endpoint has only boundedly many geometric outputs after the reductions, contradicting arbitrarily many distinct upper types.
- **claim-multiplicative-inner-order-quotients** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-grw-indices)): The positive integers $$e_{ij}=\|P_{ij}\|/\|T_i\|$$ satisfy $e_{ik}=e_{ij}e_{jk}$ for every $i<j<k$. They multiply in the same way through each selected shortcut.
  - Explanation: Equal-multiplicity saturation makes the inner order quotients positive integers that multiply through chain comparisons and selected shortcuts.
- **claim-coordinate-soluble-and-commuting-tests** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-grw-normal-commuting)): Let $$z_i/F_j\le\overline U<z_j/F_j$$ be an actual subgroup, and let $U$ be its full inverse image in $z_j$. A transported product normal in $\overline U$ is called *killed* if it is contained in $D/F_j$; it then lies in $\operatorname{core}_{\overline U}(D/F_j)$.* 1. * If $\widehat R\trianglelefteq\overline U$ is soluble, then $$\label{grw:normal-containment} \widehat R\le D/F_j,\qquad R\le P_{ij}.$$* 2. *Let $R,Q\le T_j$ be $M_{ij}$-invariant, with $\widehat R,\widehat Q$ normal in the same $\overline U$. Suppose that $$\label{grw:commuting-kernel} [\widehat R,\widehat Q]\le\overline K \trianglelefteq\overline U,\qquad \overline K\le D/F_j.$$ Then at least one of $\widehat R,\widehat Q$ is killed, and its coordinate subgroup is contained in $P_{ij}$.
  - Explanation: In the same actual proper enlargement, soluble transported normal products are killed, and commuting normal products modulo a bottom-contained normal kernel force at least one product to be killed.
- **claim-small-stabilizer-parabolic-obstruction** (bound, [source](#stmt-grw-small-parabolic)): There is an absolute constant $c_0>0$ with the following property. Let $T$ be a classical simple group of sufficiently large natural dimension $n$, over parameter $q=p^f$, and let $M\le\operatorname{Aut}(T)$ have order $m$. If $$n>2(m^2+m),$$ then $M$ normalizes a proper parabolic subgroup of $T$ whose unipotent radical has order at least $q^{c_0 n}$. Consequently the coordinate normal test excludes $M=M_{ij}$ whenever, in addition, $q_j^{c_0 n_j}>\|M_{ij}\|$.
  - Explanation: A sufficiently small automorphism subgroup relative to natural dimension normalizes a proper parabolic with a large radical; the additional radical-order comparison makes this incompatible with the coordinate normal test.
- **claim-crossing-tower-growth** (bound, [source](#stmt-grw-towers)): Suppose every comparison in a reduced homogeneous chain has a crossing. For every fixed $h,C$ and every sufficiently distant pair $i<j$, $$n_j>\mathcal E_h(a_i^C).$$ The required distance is a constant depending only on $h,C$ and the constants in the catalogue. Also $n_j>a_i^C$ for every fixed $C$ after a fixed separation and a sufficiently large minimum rank.
  - Explanation: Repeated crossings force natural dimensions beyond any fixed-height tower in the lower group order after uniformly bounded separation.
- **claim-defining-characteristic-preservation** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-grw-no-crossing)): After passage to a reduced homogeneous chain, neither cover of any comparison changes the defining characteristic.
  - Explanation: After homogeneous reduction, every selected cover preserves the defining characteristic.
- **claim-common-field-quadratic-growth** (bound, [source](#stmt-grw-common-field)): On the remaining arbitrarily long chains, the endpoints can be taken to have one common family and one common field $q=p^f$. The intermediate field ratios belong to a fixed finite set of positive rationals. In particular, all extension and twisted-tensor degrees in these paths are bounded integers. Every comparison satisfies $$\label{grw:quadratic-growth} n_j\ge c n_i^2.$$
  - Explanation: The remaining chains can share family and field, while intermediate field ratios and exceptional degrees are bounded and every comparison grows at least quadratically.
- **claim-large-radical-cover-exclusion** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-grw-no-parabolic-cover)): After a further homogeneous reduction, no selected shortcut contains a parabolic or subspace cover with a large unipotent radical.
  - Explanation: Homogeneous index comparisons eliminate selected parabolic or subspace covers with large unipotent radicals.
- **claim-remaining-inner-order-bound** (bound, [source](#stmt-grw-inner-order)): For the remaining shortcuts there is an absolute $C$ such that $$\label{grw:inner-small} \|P_{ij}\|\le q^{C n_i^2}.$$
  - Explanation: Remaining inner projection orders are bounded in terms of the common field and the lower natural dimension.
- **claim-retained-common-field-path-configuration** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-grw-remaining-paths)): If the reduced chains of Proposition <a href="#cls:reduction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cls:reduction">25</a> have arbitrary length, then they still have arbitrary length subject to all of the following properties.* 1. *The endpoints have a common classical family and field $q=p^f$, their natural dimensions tend to infinity, and their common factor multiplicity is $m$. Every selected shortcut has one active factor at each cover and no other nonabelian factor in its inner projection.* 2. *Every selected two-edge shortcut contains a defining-characteristic nonlinear cover. Its representation is a single Frobenius digit after the twisted-tensor geometric alternative has been separated. The other cover is another such nonlinear cover, or a block, form, tensor, extension-field, subfield, or twisted-tensor cover. No crossing, symplectic-type cover, or parabolic cover with a large unipotent radical remains. The characteristic-two nonsingular-line form inclusion is retained, with its natural simple quotient convention.* 3. *There are fixed constants $b,C$ and a fixed finite set $\mathcal R\subset\mathbb Q_{>0}$ such that every intermediate exponent satisfies $f'/f\in\mathcal R$, every field-extension or twisted-tensor degree is at most $b$, and every inactive geometric natural dimension is at most $b$. In particular each remaining geometric cover satisfies $n_{\mathrm{target}}\le C(1+n_{\mathrm{source}})^b$.* 4. *There are fixed $c,C>0$ such that $$n_j\ge c n_i^2,\qquad \|P_{ij}\|\le q^{C n_i^2}.$$ For any prescribed exponent $d$, fixed-spacing thinning gives also $n_j\ge n_i^d$ for every retained pair, after raising the minimum rank.* 5. *The coordinate normal tests of Lemma <a href="#grw:coordinate-normal-tests" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="grw:coordinate-normal-tests">[grw:coordinate-normal-tests]</a> remain available for every tested proper coordinate overgroup. After one more fixed-spacing thinning, $M_{ij}$ normalizes no proper parabolic of $T_j$.
  - Explanation: The retained chains preserve arbitrary length while acquiring common-field endpoints, nonlinear shortcuts, bounded geometric data, dimension and order estimates, and proper-parabolic exclusion.
- **claim-quasisimple-component-preimage** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-lift-component-preimage)): Suppose $P_0\leq P_1$, $E_1\lhd P_1$ is quasisimple, and $P_1/E_1$ is soluble. Let $\pi:P_1\longrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}(E_1)$ be conjugation. Suppose that $\overline P_0=\pi(P_0)$ has a normal quasisimple subgroup $\overline E_0$ with soluble quotient. Then $$E_0=P_0^{(\infty)}\leq E_1$$ is quasisimple and $P_0/E_0$ is soluble. In particular $E_0$ is normalized by every group normalizing $P_0$.
  - Explanation: A normal quasisimple subgroup in the conjugation image, with soluble quotient, lifts to the terminal derived subgroup inside the higher component; a mere composition-factor count would not suffice.
- **claim-uniform-standard-finite-covers** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-lift-finite-covers)): There is an absolute rank bound, independent of the finite field, with the following property. Let $\mathbf G$ be a simply connected classical algebraic group above this bound, let $\sigma$ be a standard split or graph-twisted Steinberg map, and put $U=\mathbf G^\sigma$. Then $U$ is perfect, $H_2(U,\mathbb Z)=0$, and its standard simple quotient map $u:U\twoheadrightarrow S$ is central. For any quasisimple central extension $a:L\twoheadrightarrow S$, there is a unique homomorphism $\pi:U\to L$ satisfying $a\pi=u$. It is surjective and has central kernel. A specified projective representation of $L$ also lifts uniquely to a linear representation of $U$ over an algebraically closed field.
  - Explanation: Above an absolute rank threshold, standard simply connected fixed-point groups provide unique surjective central lifts to quasisimple covers and unique linear lifts of specified projective representations.
- **claim-first-cohomology-restriction-injectivity** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-lift-h1-restriction)): Let $\mathbf G$ be a simply connected simple algebraic group over an algebraically closed field $k$ of characteristic $p$. Let $\sigma=F_q\gamma$, where $q=p^f\geq2$ and $\gamma$ is a standard diagram automorphism commuting with $F_q$. For every nonzero $q$-restricted dominant weight $\nu$, restriction is injective: $$H^1(\mathbf G,L(\nu))\longrightarrow H^1(\mathbf G^\sigma,L(\nu)).$$
  - Explanation: First cohomology restriction is injective for each nonzero restricted highest weight, including the diagram-twisted fixed-point groups under the stated hypotheses.
- **claim-prescribed-quadratic-form-lift** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-lift-quadratic)): Let $k$ have characteristic two and let $\mathbf G$, $q$, and $\sigma$ be as in Lemma <a href="#lift:h1-restriction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lift:h1-restriction">45</a>. Suppose that $V=L(\nu)$ is nontrivial and $q$-restricted, and that its restriction to $\mathbf G^\sigma$ is irreducible and preserves a nonzero quadratic form $Q$. If $V$ is not the natural module for a group isomorphic to $\operatorname{Sp}_{2n}$, $n\geq1$, then the rational action of $\mathbf G$ preserves the same quadratic form $Q$.
  - Explanation: In characteristic two, a prescribed finite invariant quadratic form lifts to the rational action for the stated restricted irreducible module, excluding the natural symplectic case.
- **claim-nonsingular-line-stabilizer-structure** (classification, [source](#stmt-lift-nonsingular-line)): Let $(W,Q)$ be a nonsingular quadratic space of even dimension $2r+2$ over $\mathbb F_q$, where $r\geq3$ and $q$ is even, and let $v\in W$ satisfy $Q(v)\neq0$. Write $B$ for the polar form and $\overline W=v^\perp/\langle v\rangle$. The kernel of $$O(W,Q)_{\langle v\rangle}\longrightarrow \operatorname{Sp}(\overline W,B)$$ is the central group generated by the symmetry $$r_v(x)=x+\frac{B(x,v)}{Q(v)}v.$$ The image is the full symplectic group. The symmetry has nonzero Dickson invariant, and restriction gives $$\Omega(W,Q)_{\langle v\rangle} \cong\operatorname{Sp}_{2r}(q).$$ In particular this stabilizer has no nontrivial finite unipotent kernel on $\overline W$. Over an algebraic closure, the vector stabilizer $\operatorname{SO}(W,Q)_v$ is a smooth connected adjoint group of type $B_r$. The ambient module $W$ restricted to this group has composition factors $k,N_{B_r},k$ along the flag $\langle v\rangle<v^\perp<W$.
  - Explanation: The finite orthogonal line stabilizer has the specified symmetry kernel and full symplectic image; its inner restriction is an isomorphism. The algebraic vector stabilizer has the stated adjoint structure and natural-module filtration.
- **claim-components-and-rational-edge-lifts** (construction, [source](#stmt-lift-edge-lifts)): In the setting of Proposition <a href="#grw:remaining-paths" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="grw:remaining-paths">41</a>, each retained projected subgroup $P$ has a characteristic normal quasisimple subgroup $L=P^{(\infty)}$ and $P/L$ is soluble. In a fixed higher coordinate, these components nest with the projected subgroups and are normalized by their common bottom action. All intermediate components of a shortcut are normalized by its lower coordinate stabilizer. The transported product of an active component maps onto the lower nonabelian socle and is not contained in the common bottom.* *For every retained geometric or defining-characteristic almost-simple edge, its actual inclusion on these components has a rational lift between their simple classical algebraic groups, after passage to simply connected central covers. The lift agrees with the finite inclusion after the specified central quotients.* *On a geometric edge, every nontrivial absolute composition factor of the target natural module is a tensor product of Frobenius twists of the source natural simple module or its dual. The number of tensor factors is uniformly bounded by the constants in Proposition <a href="#grw:remaining-paths" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="grw:remaining-paths">41</a>. Trivial factors and repeated copies are allowed. For type $B$ in characteristic two, “natural simple module” means the $2r$-dimensional quotient of the usual $(2r+1)$-dimensional module.
  - Explanation: Retained structures supply actual characteristic quasisimple components, nested finite inclusions, and compatible rational edge lifts through central covers. Geometric natural constituents have the stated tensor description.
- **claim-pathwise-rational-lift** (construction, [source](#stmt-lift-path-lifts)): Fix a path through retained edges with finite nested components $L_0\leq\cdots\leq L_s$. Choose an edge lift $\phi_i:\mathbf G_i\to\mathbf G_{i+1}$ from Proposition <a href="#lift:edge-lifts" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lift:edge-lifts">49</a> for each edge, with the finite central-cover identifications specified there. Then $$\Phi_{i,j}=\phi_{j-1}\cdots\phi_i\qquad(i<j)$$ is a rational lift of the actual finite inclusion along that path. If a rational $\mathbf G_j$-module is irreducible on $L_i$ under this finite inclusion, it is irreducible on the algebraic image $\Phi_{i,j}(\mathbf G_i)$. A nontrivial such image is a closed connected simple algebraic group; if its rank is strictly smaller than the rank of $\mathbf G_j$, it is proper.
  - Explanation: Chosen edge lifts compose along a specified path. Finite irreducibility implies irreducibility on the containing algebraic image, and strict rank inequality gives properness.
- **claim-backward-geometric-irreducibility** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-lift-geometric-irreducibility)): Suppose that a retained geometric edge has source component $L$, and that the target natural module restricts absolutely irreducibly and nontrivially to a subgroup $H\leq L$. Then the source natural simple module restricts absolutely irreducibly to $H$.
  - Explanation: Absolute irreducibility of the target natural restriction passes backwards to the source natural simple module along a retained geometric edge.
- **claim-no-invariant-proper-parabolic** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-pkt-no-parabolic)): After passing to a fixed-spacing subchain, no comparison stabilizer $M_{ij}$ normalizes a proper parabolic subgroup of $T_j$.
  - Explanation: Fixed-spacing thinning leaves no proper parabolic normalized by a comparison stabilizer.
- **claim-semisimple-natural-section** (classification, [source](#stmt-pkt-semisimple)): Let $V$ be the upper natural module in a retained comparison. As a module for the lower quasisimple component, either $V$ is semisimple, or the characteristic is two, $V$ is an even-dimensional quadratic space, and there is an $M$-invariant nonsingular line $R$ such that $$V^{\circ}=R^\perp/R$$ is a semisimple symplectic module. In the latter case the composition length of $V$ is that of $V^{\circ}$ plus two. The lower component and its soluble-quotient and normal-subgroup properties pass to $V^{\circ}$.
  - Explanation: The natural restriction is semisimple except for the stated characteristic-two nonsingular-line case. Passing to its symplectic quotient removes only the specified trivial factors and preserves the structural normal tests.
- **claim-soluble-active-component-centralizer** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-pkt-centralizer)): The centralizer of the lower quasisimple component in the inner classical group on $V$ is soluble.
  - Explanation: The commuting-normal test and the soluble quotient of the active component force its inner classical centralizer to be soluble.
- **claim-absolute-constituent-multiplicity-bound** (bound, [source](#stmt-pkt-multiplicity)): Every absolute irreducible constituent of $V$ has multiplicity at most $15$.
  - Explanation: Every absolute constituent has bounded multiplicity because higher multiplicity would create a nonsoluble inner subgroup in the centralizer.
- **claim-at-most-one-large-packet** (bound, [source](#stmt-pkt-one-packet)): Two disjoint unions of packets on which $E$ acts nontrivially cannot both have dimension at least $16$. Consequently either one packet accounts for all but at most $15$ dimensions, or the sum of all nontrivial packets has dimension at most $45$.
  - Explanation: Disjoint nontrivial packet unions cannot both be large. This bounds the complement of a large packet or the total nontrivial dimension when all packets are small.
- **claim-field-shift-synchronization** (bound, [source](#stmt-pkt-field-shifts)): Let the endpoint exponent be $f$, and let the intermediate exponent on a remaining shortcut be $$f'=\frac uv f,\qquad (u,v)=1.$$ Put $h=\gcd(f,f')=f/v$. If an element of $M$ induces source field exponent $a$ and upper scalar exponent $s$, then $$s-a\equiv0\pmod h,\qquad v(s-a)\equiv0\pmod f. \label{pkt:shift-congruence}$$ Every packet of absolute constituent types has size at most $2v$.
  - Explanation: The source field action and upper scalar action agree modulo the common divisor of endpoint and intermediate exponents. Their synchronized action bounds packet size by the field-ratio denominator.
- **claim-uniform-absolute-composition-length** (bound, [source](#stmt-pkt-bounded-length)): In the setting of Proposition <a href="#grw:remaining-paths" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="grw:remaining-paths">41</a>, let $B$ be an absolute bound for the denominators of the intermediate field ratios $f'/f$ on the remaining shortcuts. After a further fixed-spacing thinning, every upper natural module, restricted to a lower active quasisimple component, has at most $$L=30B+62$$ absolute composition factors, counted with multiplicity. The bound uses neither natural-module irreducibility between endpoints nor an irreducible-triples theorem.
  - Explanation: Multiplicity, packet-size, and remainder bounds yield a uniform absolute composition-length bound without assuming endpoint irreducibility or using irreducible triples.
- **claim-ambient-rank-bound-from-length** (bound, [source](#stmt-irr-rank-length)): Let $H<Y$ be connected classical simple algebraic groups with $r=\operatorname{rk}(H)\geq9$. Suppose $V$ is a nontrivial irreducible, $p$-restricted, tensor-indecomposable $Y$-module which is not of natural type, and $V\|_H$ is irreducible. If $\ell_H(N_Y)\leq c$ for an integer $c\geq1$, then $$\operatorname{rk}(Y)\in \mathcal R(r)\cup\{tr,tr+1:2\leq t\leq c\}.$$ In particular the number of possible ambient ranks is at most $2c+7$. The assertion is unchanged by central covers and the isogenies in <a href="#irr:bc-weights" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="irr:bc-weights">[irr:bc-weights]</a>.
  - Explanation: The corrected irreducible-triple classification bounds possible ambient ranks when the natural restriction has bounded composition length, retaining the diagonal spin alternatives only within that length bound.
- **claim-ambient-rank-bound-with-intervening-group** (bound, [source](#stmt-irr-intervening)): Let $H<X<Y$ be connected classical simple algebraic groups with $r=\operatorname{rk}(H)\geq9$ and $s=\operatorname{rk}(X)>r$. Suppose $N_X\|_H$ is irreducible. If $V$ is a nontrivial irreducible, $p$-restricted, tensor-indecomposable $Y$-module, not of natural type, and $V\|_H$ is irreducible, then $$\operatorname{rk}(Y)\in\mathcal R(r).$$ The same conclusion holds when $X=Y$ and $N_Y\|_H$ is irreducible.
  - Explanation: An intervening group of strictly larger rank with irreducible natural restriction eliminates the unbounded diagonal spin alternatives. The stated endpoint case also applies.
- **claim-stabilized-factor-count-rigidity** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-irr-constituent-count)): Suppose that, for every $i<j$ in a chain of quasisimple components, the restriction $N_j\|_{L_i}$ has exactly $a$ nontrivial and $b$ trivial composition factors. Assume $a\geq1$ and that every nontrivial simple $L_j$-constituent restricts nontrivially to each earlier $L_i$. For every $i<j<k$, each nontrivial composition factor of $N_k\|_{L_j}$ restricts irreducibly and nontrivially to $L_i$.
  - Explanation: Constant trivial and nontrivial composition counts, together with nontrivial restriction of each constituent, force every intermediate nontrivial factor to restrict irreducibly.
- **claim-absolutely-irreducible-natural-endpoint-subchains** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-irr-natural-endpoints)): In the remaining configurations of Proposition <a href="#grw:remaining-paths" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="grw:remaining-paths">41</a>, arbitrarily long chains have arbitrarily long subchains on which every natural endpoint module restricts absolutely irreducibly to each earlier endpoint.
  - Explanation: Ramsey stabilization of factor counts and the ambient-rank bound produce arbitrarily long subchains with absolutely irreducible natural endpoint restrictions.
- **claim-restricted-natural-product-collapse** (classification, [source](#stmt-irr-restricted-natural)): Let $J$ be a classical simple algebraic group of rank at least nine. Let $M$ be a nontrivial $p$-restricted simple $J$-module. If every nontrivial tensor-indecomposable factor of $M$ is of natural type, then $M\cong N_J$ or $N_J^*$. In particular there is exactly one nontrivial terminal factor and $\dim M=n(J)$.
  - Explanation: A restricted simple module whose terminal tensor factors are all natural type must be a single natural or dual-natural module, since a product of multiple such factors is reducible.
- **claim-natural-tail-irreducibility-transport** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-irr-natural-tail)): Consider an edge between the finite components associated with algebraic sources $J$ and $K$. Suppose every nontrivial absolute composition factor of the target natural module, restricted to the source, is a tensor product of natural-type $J$-modules. If that target module is absolutely irreducible on an earlier noncentral quasisimple component $L$, then $N_J\|_L$ is absolutely irreducible. This applies to each retained geometric edge and to every one-digit edge whose restricted terminal factors are all of natural type.
  - Explanation: Absolute irreducibility on an earlier noncentral component passes backwards through a target restriction built from natural-type tensor factors, covering retained geometric and the stated one-digit edges.
- **claim-finite-decorated-lattice** (construction, [source](#stmt-lat-decorated-lattice)): There is a finite nonempty lattice $L$ with the following properties. The properties hold in either orientation of $L$, using the corresponding Boolean and detector components.* 1. *The lattice contains a bounded copy of the original $B_4$. Every proper nonzero original Boolean vertex $v$ has both $[0,v]$ and $[v,1]$ fenced. The global interval $[0,1]$ is fenced.* 2. *There are original detector vertices $d_1,d_2,X,z$ with $0<d_i<X<z<1$. The intervals $[0,d_i]$, $[0,X]$, $[X,1]$ and $[z,1]$ are fenced. Every coatom of $[0,X]$ is above a $d_i$.* 3. *In any finite subgroup-interval representation $L\cong[D,G]$, the simple labels of every proper nonzero original Boolean vertex, of $d_1,d_2$, and of $X$ equal the simple label of $G$.* 4. *Let $0<v<u<1$ be comparable original Boolean vertices. In any finite subgroup-interval representation $$[v,1]^{\mathrm{op}}\cong[A,U_v],$$ the labels of the vertices corresponding to $u$ and $v$, taken relative to the common bottom $A$, are defined and equal. The same assertion holds for the detector pair $(z,X)$ in any representation $[X,1]^{\mathrm{op}}\cong[A,U_X]$.* *In (iv), no representation of the entire dual lattice is assumed. If several such upper filters have compatible realizations with a common bottom $A$, the conclusions hold in that compatible system.
  - Explanation: The finite decorated lattice preserves the original Boolean operations and carries forward and reverse tests, fences, and detector data in either orientation. Reverse conclusions concern actual upper-filter representations.
- **claim-private-insertion-lattice-preservation** (construction, [source](#stmt-lat-insertion)): A private insertion gives a finite lattice and preserves all old meets and joins. If $w$ is a fresh interior vertex and $v$ is an old vertex, then $$\label{lat:cross-order} v\leq w\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v\leq a, \qquad w\leq v\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad b\leq v.$$ An old cover $c\prec d$ is destroyed by the insertion if and only if the insertion has endpoints $a=c$, $b=d$ and has a nonempty interior.
  - Explanation: A private bounded-lattice insertion preserves old meets and joins, fixes cross comparisons through its endpoints, and destroys an old cover only when it inserts a nonempty interior into that exact cover.
- **claim-permanent-fence-under-insertions** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-lat-persistent-fence)): Suppose the proper part of an interval $[a,b]$ has two different components in its comparability graph, each containing two strictly comparable vertices. Then $[a,b]$ is fenced. This property persists under any finite sequence of private insertions into the surrounding lattice. In particular, a fencing insertion makes an interval fenced permanently.
  - Explanation: Separate proper comparability components containing comparable pairs supply a fence, and private insertions preserve those components and their witnesses.
- **claim-finite-protected-shape-batches** (construction, [source](#stmt-lat-shape)): The five batches are finite and have the following properties.* 1. *Every designated shortcut has both edges as covers.* 2. *Every $[x_i,x_j]$ is fenced. For every $u\in\mathcal U$, $[a,u]$ is fenced, $a$ is a meet of coatoms below $u$, and $a<m_u$ with $[m_u,u]\cong M_{16}$.* 3. *Every vertex in $\mathcal C$ is a meet of coatoms below $b$. Each $v_{iN}$ is itself a coatom below $b$.* *No interval $[a,v_{0j}]$ is included in the extra target operations. The construction introduces at most $27N^2$ vertices.
  - Explanation: The finite shape batches preserve designated shortcut covers, create the required fences and exact height-two tests, and supply coatom witnesses within the stated vertex bound.
- **claim-simultaneous-forward-reverse-tests** (construction, [source](#stmt-lat-simultaneous)): For either component $C_N$, all the following statements hold.* 1. *Every forward shape test retains all conclusions of Lemma <a href="#lat:shape" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lat:shape">69</a>. Its principal vertices other than $1$ have fenced intervals from $0$.* 2. *Every reverse shape test retains all conclusions of Lemma <a href="#lat:shape" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lat:shape">69</a> in the reverse order. Every vertex in each of its comparison intervals has a fenced interval from the reverse base $1$.* 3. *For a forward chosen chain and any $i<j$, every vertex $t\in[x_i,x_j]$, except possibly $t=1$, satisfies one of the following alternatives:* 1. *$[0,t]$ is fenced;* 2. *there is a vertex $s$ with $x_i\leq s<t$, with $[0,s]$ fenced, such that every vertex of $[0,t]$ is comparable to $s$.* 4. *In the detector the coatoms of $[0,X]$ are exactly $q_1,q_2$. In particular, each contains one of $d_1,d_2$ below it. The intervals $[0,X]$ and $[X,1]$ remain fenced.* *The construction is finite. If $C$ has $q_0$ vertices and altogether $h$ requested pairs in the two directions, then $$\|C_N\|\leq9(q_0+27hN^2).$$
  - Explanation: Disjoint shape interiors and the frozen final batch preserve forward and reverse tests simultaneously, provide labelled bottlenecks for new forward comparison vertices, and retain the detector coatom condition.
- **claim-almost-simple-normal-subgroups** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-ext-almost-simple)): Let $T$ be a finite nonabelian simple group and let $\operatorname{Inn}(T)\le H\le\operatorname{Aut}(T)$. Every nontrivial normal subgroup of $H$ contains $\operatorname{Inn}(T)$. In particular, $H$ has trivial soluble radical and has characteristic socle $\operatorname{Inn}(T)$.
  - Explanation: A group between the inner and full automorphism groups of a finite nonabelian simple group has its inner group inside every nontrivial normal subgroup, hence trivial soluble radical.
- **claim-soluble-group-fence-exclusion** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-ext-soluble-interval)): A nontrivial fenced interval cannot be an interval in a finite soluble group. Consequently, if $\operatorname{Inn}(T)\le B\le H\le\operatorname{Aut}(T)$, the interval $[B,H]$ is not nontrivially fenced.
  - Explanation: Finite soluble groups cannot contain nontrivial fenced intervals; quotienting an almost simple interval with the inner group in its bottom gives the same obstruction.
- **claim-minimal-complementary-socle** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-ext-trivial-intersection)): In this minimal representation, $D\cap S=1$.
  - Explanation: Minimum group order over both lattice orientations forces the bottom to intersect the top socle trivially.
- **claim-subdirect-extension-dictionary** (construction, [source](#stmt-ext-dictionary)): Let a finite group $D$ act on $S=\prod_{i\in I}T_i$, where all $T_i$ are isomorphic to a nonabelian simple group $T$, and suppose that its action on $I$ is transitive. Fix $i_0\in I$, set $A=D_{i_0}$, identify $T_{i_0}$ with $T$, and let $\alpha:A\to\operatorname{Aut}(T)$ be the induced action.* *The $D$-invariant subdirect subgroups of $S$ are in bijection with pairs $(U,\beta)$, where $$A\le U\le D,\qquad \beta:U\longrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}(T),\qquad \beta\|_A=\alpha.$$ Write $S(U,\beta)$ for the corresponding subgroup. Then $$\label{ext:dictionary-order} S(U,\beta)\le S(V,\gamma) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad V\le U\ \hbox{ and }\ \beta\|_V=\gamma.$$ In particular, the interval of $D$-invariant subgroups from $S(U,\beta)$ to $S$ is anti-isomorphic to $[A,U]$, by restricting $\beta$.
  - Explanation: Invariant subdirect groups correspond to actual homomorphism extensions on factor-block stabilizers. Inclusion reverses domain containment and enforces restriction of the homomorphisms.
- **claim-detector-full-inner-image** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-ext-detector)): In the minimal representation fixed above, the induced factor-stabilizer action $\alpha$ satisfies $\alpha(A)\ge\operatorname{Inn}(T)$.
  - Explanation: The detector and its reverse test force the factor-stabilizer image to contain the entire inner automorphism group.
- **claim-fenced-extension-constant-image** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-ext-constant-image)): With $\alpha$ as in Proposition <a href="#ext:detector" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ext:detector">75</a>, let $A<U\le D$ and let $\beta:U\to\operatorname{Aut}(T)$ extend $\alpha$. Suppose that $[A,U]$ is fenced. Then $$U=A\ker\beta, \qquad \beta(U)=\alpha(A).$$
  - Explanation: An extension on a fenced domain supplements the bottom by its kernel and has the same image as the bottom action.
- **claim-boolean-extension-obstruction-configuration** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-ext-e4)): If either orientation of the decorated lattice has a finite-group interval representation, there are finite groups $A\le D$, finite nonabelian simple groups $T,R$, a homomorphism $\alpha:A\to\operatorname{Aut}(T)$, and extensions $$\beta_J:U_J\to\operatorname{Aut}(T) \qquad(\varnothing\ne J\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,4\})$$ with the following properties. Set $U_\varnothing=A$ and $\beta_\varnothing=\alpha$.* 1. * For nonempty proper $J$, $[A,U_J]$ is fenced. If $C_J=\operatorname{core}_{U_J}(A)$, the group $U_J/C_J$ has unique minimal normal subgroup $$N_J/C_J\cong R^{I_J},\qquad U_J=AN_J.$$* 2. * If $J\subsetneq K\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,4\}$, then $U_J<U_K$ and $\beta_K\|_{U_J}=\beta_J$. For nonempty $J$, the equal-type transport of Proposition <a href="#frm:equal-transport" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="frm:equal-transport">8</a> applies: in particular $$\frac{U_J\cap N_K}{C_K}\ \cong\ \frac{N_J}{C_J}, \qquad N_J=(U_J\cap N_K)C_J,$$ and the canonical surjections $I_K\to I_J$ are $U_J$-equivariant and compose. Whenever a nonempty family of proper subsets has proper union $K$, its domains generate $U_K$.* 3. * All images $\beta_J(U_J)$ equal $H=\alpha(A)\ge\operatorname{Inn}(T)$.* 4. *If a family of proper nonempty subsets has union $\{1,\ldots,4\}$, its homomorphisms have no common extension to the subgroup of $D$ generated by their domains.
  - Explanation: A finite-group representation would supply compatible extensions on proper Boolean domains with a common inner-containing image and equal domain socle types, while full unions forbid a common extension.
- **claim-perfect-image-intersections** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-glue-perfect-intersections)): Let $f:M\to H_0$ be a homomorphism of finite groups, let $P\le H_0$ be perfect, and let $B_1,\ldots,B_s\trianglelefteq M$, with $s\ge1$, satisfy $P\le f(B_i)$ for every $i$. Then $$P\le f\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^s B_i\right).$$
  - Explanation: Finite intersections of normal subgroups retain a perfect subgroup contained in each individual image.
- **claim-common-core-conjugation-extension** (construction, [source](#stmt-glue-common-core)): Let $A\le U_i\le D$ be a finite nonempty family of subgroups of a finite group. Let $T$ be nonabelian simple and suppose that homomorphisms $$\alpha:A\to\operatorname{Aut}(T),\qquad \beta_i:U_i\to\operatorname{Aut}(T)$$ satisfy $$\beta_i\|_A=\alpha, \qquad \alpha\bigl(\operatorname{core}_{U_i}(A)\bigr) \ge\operatorname{Inn}(T).$$ Put $K=\langle U_i:i\rangle$. Then $\alpha(\operatorname{core}_K(A))\ge\operatorname{Inn}(T)$, and there is a unique homomorphism $\beta:K\to\operatorname{Aut}(T)$ extending all the $\beta_i$.
  - Explanation: When each domain core maps over the inner group, a least normal subgroup with that perfect image is normal in the generated domain. Its conjugation action supplies the unique common extension.
- **claim-killed-atom-core-permutation-factorization** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-glue-factorization)): If $x$ is an original Boolean atom and $\alpha(C_x)=1$, then $\beta_x$ factors through the permutation action of $U_x$ on $I_x$.
  - Explanation: If an atom core has trivial image, its extension kills the socle and then the soluble factor-action kernel, leaving only the permutation action on the socle factors.
- **claim-compatible-fiber-lifts** (construction, [source](#stmt-glue-lifts)): For $u\in\mathcal U_x$ and $j\in I_x$, define $$\label{glue:Luj} L_{u,j}=N_u(F_{u,j})\cap \bigcap_{\substack{v\in\mathcal U_x\\v\ne u}} \bigl(U_u\cap N_{u\cup v}(F_{u\cup v,j})\bigr).$$ These subgroups have the following properties.* 1. *They are normal in $N_u$, and $q_u(L_{u,j})=\prod_{i\in F_{u,j}}S_{u,i}$.* 2. *Conjugation by $U_x$ permutes the choices according to its action on $I_x$. In particular, $C_x$ normalizes every $L_{u,j}$.* 3. *$U_u=\langle A,L_{u,j}:j\in I_x\rangle$.* 4. *For $j\ne k$, one has $$[L_{u,j},L_{v,k}]\le \begin{cases} C_{u\cup v},&u\ne v,\\ C_u,&u=v. \end{cases}$$ Both right-hand sides are contained in $C_x$.* 5. *If $\alpha(C_x)=1$, then $\beta_u(L_{u,j})=1$ for all $u,j$.
  - Explanation: Intersecting support preimages across proper pair joins constructs normal lifts retaining each fiber image, with equivariance, generation, controlled cross-label commutators, and trivial extension images in the killed-core case.
- **claim-core-retains-simple-image** (construction, [source](#stmt-glue-retained-core)): Let $R_0\le D$, let $C\trianglelefteq R_0$, and suppose that $R_0/C$ is nonabelian simple. Let $L_1,\ldots,L_s\le D$ be normalized by $R_0$. Suppose that, for every $t$, there is a subgroup $D_t\trianglelefteq R_0$ such that $$D_tC=R_0,\qquad D_t^{L_t}=D_t, \qquad [D_t,L_t]\le D_t\cap C.$$ Then, for $W=\langle R_0,L_1,\ldots,L_s\rangle$, the subgroup $\operatorname{core}_W(R_0)$ maps onto $R_0/C$. No normalization of $C$ by $L_t$ is assumed.
  - Explanation: Repeated finite core operations retain a full simple image and stabilize to a normal subgroup in the generated domain, without requiring the quotient kernel to be normalized by all lifts.
- **claim-canonical-factor-label-detectors** (construction, [source](#stmt-glue-detectors)): Put $L_j=\langle L_{u,j}:u\in\mathcal U_x\rangle$ and $R_k=N_x(\{k\})$. There are subgroups $B_k\le R_k$, for $k\in I_x$, such that* 1. *$q_x(B_k)=S_{x,k}$;* 2. *every $L_j$ with $j\ne k$ normalizes $B_k$;* 3. *$C_x$ normalizes every $B_k$, and $A$ permutes the $B_k$ in the same way as it permutes $I_x$.* *In particular, the subgroups $B_k$ are pairwise distinct.
  - Explanation: Canonical cores of support preimages distinguish the factor labels and are normalized by all lifts of different labels, with bottom equivariance.
- **claim-labelled-word-collection** (construction, [source](#stmt-glue-collection)): Let $C\le D$ normalize subgroups $P_\lambda\le D$ indexed by a finite set. Assign each index a label $c(\lambda)\in I$. Suppose that $$[P_\lambda,P_\mu]\le C \quad\text{whenever }c(\lambda)\ne c(\mu).$$ Put $L_j=\langle P_\lambda:c(\lambda)=j\rangle$ and $L=\langle L_j:j\in I\rangle$. For every $k\in I$, every element $g\in L$ can be written $$g=pqc,\qquad p\in\langle L_j:j\ne k\rangle,\quad q\in L_k,\quad c\in C.$$
  - Explanation: Different-label letters can be collected with all commutator errors moved to the right through normalization of individual factors; no quotient by the error subgroup is needed.
- **claim-atom-cores-retain-inner-image** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-glue-atom-cores)): For every original Boolean atom $x$, $\alpha(C_x)\ge\operatorname{Inn}(T)$.
  - Explanation: A killed atom core would yield a common extension on the full union through compatible lifts and label detectors, so every atom core retains the inner image.
- **claim-compatible-join-core-intersection** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-glue-core-joins)): For every nonempty proper original Boolean node $z$, $$C_z=\bigcap_{x\subseteq z,\,\|x\|=1}C_x.$$ Consequently $\alpha(C_z)\ge\operatorname{Inn}(T)$.
  - Explanation: A proper Boolean node core equals the intersection of its atom cores. Perfect-image preservation therefore passes the inner image from atoms to every proper nonempty node.
- **claim-boolean-extension-contradiction** (theorem, [source](#stmt-glue-contradiction)): The Boolean extension configuration of Proposition <a href="#ext:reduction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ext:reduction">[ext:reduction]</a> does not exist.
  - Explanation: Proper Boolean faces retain enough common core image to force the common extension that the full-union condition forbids.

        "anchor": "stmt-frm-projection",
        "exact_quote": "Let $D\\le X<Y$, with $Y$ labelled, and suppose that $$(X\\cap N_Y)/F_Y=P_X^{I_Y},\\qquad 1<P_X<T_Y.$$ Suppose also that $X$ is an intersection of coatoms of $[X,Y]$; a coatom itself is allowed. Fix $i\\in I_Y$ and let $$\\rho:Y_i\\longrightarrow\\operatorname{Aut}(T_Y)$$ be the action of its factor stabilizer on that coordinate. Identify $T_Y$ with its inner automorphism group, and put $H_* = \\rho(X_i)$. Then $$\\label{frm:inner-bottom}\n H_*\\cap T_Y=P_X.$$ The saturated overgroups of $X$ form a sublattice of $[X,Y]$, and $$\\label{frm:coordinate-interval}\n Z\\longmapsto K_Z=\\rho(Z_i)=H_*P_Z,\n \\qquad (Z\\cap N_Y)/F_Y=P_Z^{I_Y},$$ is an isomorphism from that sublattice onto the entire ordinary subgroup interval $[H_*,H_*T_Y]$. Original covering relations between saturated vertices remain covering relations after projection.         "anchor": "stmt-frm-active-transport",
        "exact_quote": "Let $D<Z\\le Y$ be labelled vertices, and suppose that $Z$ is saturated relative to $Y$: $$(Z\\cap N_Y)/F_Y=P_Z^{I_Y}.$$ Let $K_Z$ be the automorphism group induced by a factor stabilizer in $Z$ on a reference coordinate of $S_Y$. There are $K_Z$-normal subgroups $Q_Z\\le R_Z\\le P_Z$ such that $$\\begin{aligned}\n \\label{frm:product-core}\n (F_Z\\cap N_Y)/F_Y&=Q_Z^{I_Y},\\\\\n \\label{frm:product-active-preimage}\n (N_Z\\cap N_Y)/F_Y&=R_Z^{I_Y},\\\\\n \\label{frm:coordinate-chief}\n R_Z/Q_Z&\\cong T_Z^{a_Z},\\qquad m_Z=a_Zm_Y.\n\\end{aligned}$$ Here $a_Z$ is a positive integer. The section $R_Z/Q_Z$ is a chief factor for the action of $K_Z$ on $P_Z$: there is no $K_Z$-normal subgroup strictly between $Q_Z$ and $R_Z$. Its factors give a $Z$-equivariant surjection $$\\label{frm:product-support}\n \\tau_{ZY}:I_Z\\longrightarrow I_Y$$ whose fibers have size $a_Z$. The stabilizers in $D$ and $Z$ of a coordinate in $I_Y$ induce the same transitive action on its fiber.*\n\n*In addition, suppose $X<Z$ and the hypotheses of Proposition <a href=\"#frm:projection\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"frm:projection\">10</a> hold for $X<Y$. Set $$H_* = \\rho(X_i),\\qquad K_Z=H_*P_Z,\n \\qquad C_Z=\\operatorname{core}_{K_Z}(H_*).$$ Then the subgroups in <a href=\"#frm:product-core\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"frm:product-core\">[frm:product-core]</a> satisfy $$\\label{frm:projected-core}\n Q_Z=C_Z\\cap P_Z,\n \\qquad K_Z=H_*R_Z.$$ Thus $R_ZC_Z/C_Z\\cong R_Z/Q_Z$ is a transitive minimal normal subgroup in the coset action of $K_Z/C_Z$ on $H_*/C_Z$. The groups $H_*$ and $K_Z$ induce the same action on its simple factors. No assertion that this is the entire projected socle is required.*\n\n*If $a_Z=1$, the quotient $P_Z/R_Z$ is soluble.",
        "source_id": "PM-206.2"

    {
      "conclusion": {
        "anchor": "stmt-cls-literature",
        "exact_quote": "The following results are used from the classification and representation theory of finite simple groups.*\n\n1.  *A maximal subgroup of an almost simple classical group, not containing its socle, is a stabilizer in one of Aschbacher’s eight geometric collections, or has an almost simple irreducible component. The geometric collections are subspace or flag stabilizers, direct-sum decompositions, extension-field structures, tensor products, subfield structures, symplectic-type groups, tensor-induced decompositions, and forms. Graph automorphisms may interchange the relevant subspaces or flag members; triality and exceptional graph–field automorphisms occur only in bounded rank. We use (Aschbacher 1984) [[Aschbacher1984](#ref-Aschbacher1984)] and the almost simple formulation and descriptions in (Kleidman and Liebeck 1990, Table 1.2.A and Theorem 1.2.1, pp. 3–4) [[KleidmanLiebeck1990](#ref-KleidmanLiebeck1990)], with the geometric descriptions in Chapters 3–5; the connected tensor structures and their finite fixed-point versions are also given in (Liebeck and Seitz 1998, Theorem 2 and Section 4(5)) [[LiebeckSeitzClassical1998](#ref-LiebeckSeitzClassical1998)].*\n\n2.  *The maximal subgroups of alternating and symmetric groups have the intransitive, imprimitive, affine, diagonal, product-action, or almost simple alternatives of the maximal-subgroup form of the O’Nan–Scott Theorem. The relevant formulation and all the alternatives used here are recorded in the proof of (Burness, Liebeck, and Shalev 2017, Proposition 3.1) [[BurnessLiebeckShalev2017](#ref-BurnessLiebeckShalev2017)].*\n\n3.  *For a fixed algebraic type, sufficiently general finite subgroups lie between the derived group and the inner-diagonal group of a finite fixed-point group. The complementary alternative is containment in a proper algebraic subgroup of bounded complexity. The bounded-envelope version permits passage to the reductive simple quotients of that subgroup; see (Larsen and Pink 2011, Theorems 0.5 and 12.3) [[LarsenPink2011](#ref-LarsenPink2011)].*\n\n4.  *A subgroup maximal in a maximal subgroup of an almost simple group has at most five nonabelian chief factors (Burness, Liebeck, and Shalev 2017, Proposition 8.1) [[BurnessLiebeckShalev2017](#ref-BurnessLiebeckShalev2017)]. The number refers to chief factors, not to their simple direct factors.*\n\n5.  *If $[H,A]$ is a height-two interval and $A$ is alternating or symmetric of degree at least five, it has at most eleven interior vertices (Basile 2001, Theorem D) [[Basile2008](#ref-Basile2008)]. Here the entire interval is required to have height two: $H$ is maximal in every maximal overgroup. This is the hypothesis imposed whenever the result is used.*\n\n6.  *Cross-characteristic irreducible projective degrees satisfy the Landazuri–Seitz lower bounds (Landazuri and Seitz 1974) [[LandazuriSeitz1974](#ref-LandazuriSeitz1974)]. In particular, outside bounded rank, a source of natural dimension $n$ and field parameter $q$ requires degree at least $q^{c n}$ for an absolute $c>0$; the applicable classical bounds are recorded in (Häsä 2014, Tables 3–6) [[Hasa2014](#ref-Hasa2014)]. Above an absolute classical rank, every perfect central cover of a finite simple classical group is a central quotient of its usual simply connected fixed-point group, uniformly over all finite fields, including the standard graph twists (Steinberg 1981, Theorem 1.1 and p. 528) [[Steinberg1981](#ref-Steinberg1981)]. The central-cover deduction and preservation of representations are proved in Lemma <a href=\"#lift:finite-covers\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"lift:finite-covers\">44</a>. After passing to that cover, defining-characteristic irreducibles have the Steinberg highest-weight and tensor-product parametrization (Steinberg 1963, Theorems 1.1 and 1.3) [[Steinberg1963](#ref-Steinberg1963)], including the twisted fixed-point groups (Steinberg 1967, Theorem 43) [[SteinbergNotes](#ref-SteinbergNotes)].",
        "source_id": "PM-206.2"
      },
      "evidence": [
        {
